questions.q: What is the most accurate way to describe the research scientist / research engineer split at major AI labs?
options: Two separate missions with almost no overlap in daily work
A center of gravity in emphasis, not a strict fence on what each role can do
A legal distinction required for visa sponsorship
An outdated split that no major lab still uses
questions.explain: Both titles serve the same mission from different angles. Labs treat the line as a spectrum of emphasis, and many people do both kinds of work.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the research engineer's more typical center of gravity?
options: Proposing novel theoretical claims for publication
Building and operating the systems that let experiments run at the needed speed and scale
Writing marketing copy for shipped models
Managing the research team's budget
questions.explain: Research engineers more often own the infrastructure — training frameworks, eval harnesses, pipelines — that experiments depend on.

questions.q: A team member is stuck for a week debugging why a distributed training run silently diverges only at 64 GPUs. This is a more typical example of which role's day-to-day friction?
options: Research scientist
Research engineer
Neither role ever encounters this
Only a dedicated SRE would see this
questions.explain: Scale-dependent infrastructure bugs like this are a classic research-engineer-flavored problem, distinct from the scientist's more typical worry about whether an idea itself is correct.

questions.q: Why do healthy research teams deliberately keep the scientist/engineer boundary soft rather than rigid?
options: Because job titles don't matter for payroll purposes
Because rigidly separating ideas people from build people tends to produce research that's untestable or uninteresting
Because it's required by labor law
Because only one title can exist per team
questions.explain: An idea nobody can test is worthless, and infrastructure not pointed at an interesting question is worthless. Keeping the line soft lets both halves of the work reinforce each other.

questions.q: Which output artifact is more typically associated with the research scientist's center of gravity, as described in this lesson?
options: A working, reproducible training pipeline
A well-supported claim, often in the form of a paper or report
A cluster job scheduler
A CI/CD pipeline
questions.explain: The research scientist's primary artifact is more often a paper, report, or well-supported claim, while the research engineer's is more often a working system.
